title: Teonanacatl: The Narcotic Mushroom of the Aztecs
author: Richard Evans Schultes
summary: Schultes's botanical account of his 1938-39 fieldwork with Blas Pablo Reko among the Mazatec, tracing the teonanácatl rediscovery from Reko's 1923 letter through Robert Weitlaner's 1936 visit to Huautla de Jiménez. Schultes identifies the mushroom as Paneolus campanulatus var. sphinctrinus.
excerpt: "In 1936, Mr Robert J. Weitlaner of Mexico City visited the capital of the Mazatec region of Oaxaca, Huautla de Jimenez, and learned of the use of certain mushrooms in witchcraft and divination among these primitive peoples."
citation: Schultes, Richard Evans. "Teonanacatl: The Narcotic Mushroom of the Aztecs." American Anthropologist, n.s., 42, no. 3, pt. 1 (July-September 1940): 429-443.

"In 1936, Mr Robert J. Weitlaner of Mexico City visited the capital of the Mazatec region of Oaxaca, Huautla de Jimenez, and learned of the use of certain mushrooms in witchcraft and divination among these primitive peoples. He secured a few samples of the narcotic plants and sent them to Reko who forwarded several pieces to the Botanical Museum of Harvard University for identification."

draft.rationale: The founding botanical paper of the field: the first peer-reviewed botanical identification of a living teonanácatl mushroom cult, and the first source to give the mushroom a Linnaean name. The article is the hinge between amateur/ethnographic reports of the 1920s-30s and the botanically rigorous work of Heim and Wasson in the 1950s. Its footnotes are the best surviving record of Robert Weitlaner's unpublished 1936 discovery at Huautla de Jiménez.
